metadata.title: Transferable lessons from analytics experts
metadata.interpretation_notice: Lessons and platform implications are research synthesis derived from the cited work. They do not imply that an expert endorses this architecture.

lessons: Treat event data and process models as formally defined analytical objects.
Keep discovery, conformance, performance analysis, simulation, and intervention as distinct composable operations.
Support case-centric and object-centric representations.
A single case identifier often destroys important relationships in complex operations.
Store event-to-object relationships first; generate cases as question-specific projections.
Qualifiers and changing object relationships must be first-class data.
A discovered process model becomes actionable only after performance, resource, queue, and scenario analysis.
Task capture requires privacy-aware instrumentation.
Simulation should compare operational redesigns rather than merely visualize current flow.
Conformance requires an explicit alignment between observed and permitted behavior.
Missing, unexpected, and reordered events require distinct deviation semantics.
A conformance score should retain the alignment evidence and cost model.
Process models need formal behavioral semantics and verification.
Syntactic validity, behavioral soundness, and empirical fit are separate tests.
Correctness and scalability must be evaluated independently.
Different process representations preserve different behavioral properties.
Model translation and simplification need semantic-preservation tests.
Visual simplicity alone is not process-model quality.
Prediction and causal estimation have different contracts.
Every causal result needs a defined estimand, identification design, assumptions, diagnostics, and uncertainty.
Overlap, balance, instruments, and discontinuities require explicit validation.
Observational analyses should emulate a clearly specified target trial when addressing treatment effects.
Eligibility, treatment, assignment, time zero, follow-up, outcome, and analysis must align.
Many biases are study-design and time-alignment failures rather than modeling failures.
Experimentation is an operational measurement system, not just a significance test.
Assignment, exposure logging, metric computation, guardrails, and stopping rules must agree.
Sample-ratio mismatch and instrumentation failures should be automatically tested.
Customer heterogeneity should be modeled rather than hidden by averages.
Lifetime value is a horizon-dependent distribution built from retention and purchase processes.
Behavioral cohorts should connect to future cash flow and uncertainty.
Separate predictive estimates from prescriptive optimization.
Objectives, constraints, costs, and uncertainty sets belong in replaceable domain assets.
Every optimization result needs feasibility, optimality, sensitivity, and solver status.
Privacy must be a composable mathematical guarantee rather than an informal promise.
Define the privacy unit and bound its contribution before applying a release mechanism.
Repeated releases consume a cumulative budget and require an immutable privacy ledger.
Analytics transformations should be modular, version-controlled, tested, documented, and reviewed.
The transformation dependency graph is a build artifact.
Business logic should use software-engineering workflows without coupling it to infrastructure internals.
Transformation DAGs need deterministic selection and incremental execution.
Environment promotion and artifact identity are part of analytics correctness.
Semantic definitions should remain above physical transformations.
Separate semantic modeling and query serving from visualization.
A metric requires expression, grain, dimensions, time semantics, and access policy.
Semantic planning must prevent ambiguous joins, fan-out, and double counting.
Lineage should use portable execution events and stable job, run, and dataset identities.
Schema and dataset versions are necessary for reliable impact analysis.
Interoperability standards should define exchange semantics without dictating internal implementations.
Data reliability is a continuous operational discipline.
Freshness, volume, distribution, schema, and lineage failures require distinct detectors.
Alerts need dependency context, ownership, severity, suppression, and incident state.
Data responsibilities should be explicit at producer-consumer boundaries.
Contracts should cover schema, semantics, quality, freshness, ownership, and compatibility.
Breaking-change detection should occur before deployment and use lineage to identify affected consumers.
An analytical engine can be embedded as a library instead of operated as a remote service.
Moving compute to local data can improve latency, privacy, and operational simplicity.
Columnar interchange is a critical boundary between analytical plans and execution engines.
Vectorized execution and columnar storage belong below the reusable analytical interface.
Portable plans are a stronger engine boundary than user-facing SQL text.
Local execution requires explicit memory, spill, concurrency, and resource controls.
Visualization is a semantic mapping from data to visual encodings rather than cosmetic output.
Interactive computation, narrative, and explanation can form one executable analytical artifact.
Units, uncertainty, provenance, truthful scales, and accessibility are correctness properties.
Feature delivery and experimental assignment should share a coordinated control plane.
Exposure records what participants actually experienced, not merely intended assignment.
Progressive rollout, targeting, experimentation, guardrails, rollback, and kill switches need distinct states.
Governed behavioral events are the foundation of product analytics.
Funnels, cohorts, retention, and journeys are different projections over the same events.
Self-service analysis still requires definitions, ownership, and versioning.
A governed warehouse can remain the operational customer source of truth.
Identity, audience formation, consent, and activation should be replaceable modules.
Destination delivery requires idempotency, durable receipts, retries, rate control, reconciliation, and repair.
Interpretable composite indicators can remain useful when their population, variables, coefficients, and calibration period are explicit.
A risk score is not automatically a calibrated probability.
Thresholds require target-population validation and drift monitoring.
Tail behavior cannot safely be inferred from averages.
Dependence under stress is not adequately summarized by ordinary correlation.
Distributional, dependency, and model uncertainty must accompany aggregated risk.
Healthcare comparisons require exposure and risk adjustment across heterogeneous populations.
Predictive accuracy does not establish that an intervention creates value.
Financial, clinical, and operational outcomes should be measured together and prospectively.
Marketing response is commonly lagged, nonlinear, saturated, and affected by external demand.
Attribution, experiments, and marketing-mix models answer different causal questions.
Decision systems need response curves, uncertainty, horizon, and extrapolation limits rather than isolated coefficients.
Supply chains should be represented as networks with coupled inventory, facility, transport, and service decisions.
Efficiency, redundancy, responsiveness, and resilience are competing objectives.
Disruption analysis needs dependency propagation, recovery times, stress scenarios, and organizational response.
Space and time must be modeled jointly for mobility and accessibility questions.
Coordinate systems, precision, aggregation units, and network travel time affect correctness.
Moving objects require trajectories, stops, paths, and temporal validity rather than static points.
People analytics should begin with an accountable organizational decision rather than available employee data.
Performance and talent measurements are produced by management systems and are not objective ground truth.
Privacy, fairness, minimum-group rules, feedback effects, and human review must be designed into the workflow.

cross_expert_principles.statement: Representation precedes algorithm selection: entities, events, objects, grain, time, units, and relationships must be correct first.
A metric is unsafe without its definition, population, unit, grain, interval, and version.
Predictive association must not be presented as causal effect without an identification design.
Optimization should consume distributions, scenarios, and sensitivities rather than unexplained point estimates.
Every component boundary needs typed inputs, outputs, compatibility, ownership, invariants, and failure semantics.
Every material result should retain data, code, assumptions, configuration, policy, and execution provenance.
Industry vocabulary and rules belong in vertical packs; reusable algorithms remain domain-neutral.
Analytics should connect evidence to decision, delivery, receipt, review, and measured outcome.
Privacy and accountable human oversight are execution properties, not post-processing additions.
Events, plans, metrics, models, lineage, and policies need portable representations.
